transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marco Li (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Meridian Head of ML), Sofia Ruiz (Meridian Platform), Liam O'Connor (Meridian CTO)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time. Quick intro, I'm Alex Morgan, AE on the account, with Priya and Marco from the SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Daniel: Good thanks, excited to see the structured output stuff - we've been wrestling with inconsistent JSON coming back from model calls.
[00:12] Priya: Awesome. Today we'll walk through JSON mode, schema enforcement, guardrails in the Console and via API, and the function/tool calling flow for sending structured order updates into your downstream systems.
[00:22] Sofia: Sounds good. For context, we're running core services on GCP, some legacy services on-prem, and we have strict PII rules and a 200ms median latency target for the order-routing endpoint.
[00:34] Marco: Great - that's helpful. We'll touch on Dedicated and VPC options as well since you mentioned on-prem.
[00:40] Alex: Quick qualification - are you planning hosted API first or jump to Dedicated?
[00:45] Liam: Prefer hosted to start but need a clear path to Dedicated/VPC within the quarter if POC looks good. Also need SOC2 controls and KMS integrations.
[00:55] Priya: Noted. Redwood supports SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM integrations for customer keys, and we can show audit logs from the Console. We'll attach the security pack after the call.
[01:05] Daniel: Perfect. Show us the JSON mode demo.
[01:10] Priya: Switching to the Console share now. (screen share) On the API side, JSON mode allows you to supply a schema - either JSON Schema or a simplified Redwood schema - and the runtime will attempt to produce strictly typed output. You can also enable strict validation which rejects outputs that don't conform, or a repair mode that attempts to coerce types.
[01:30] Marco: Example: order object with fields order_id (string), items (array of objects with sku, qty), total_amount (number), shipping_address (object with street, city, country). We'll demo the function-calling hook where a validated JSON payload gets forwarded to your webhook.
[01:50] [01:52] Daniel: Will the runtime ever hallucinate extra fields that break downstream parsers? That's a big risk for us.
[02:00] Priya: Great question. With strict validation + schema locking we can prevent extra root-level fields. The model can still produce unexpected keys inside free-form text blobs, but you'll see a validation error and the call either fails or goes to repair depending on config.
[02:20] Alex: Also we have a sanitize/strip option in the Console to remove any fields not in the schema before sending downstream.
[02:30] Sofia: Show us function calling flow. How do we hook into our downstream order service?
[02:36] Marco: We set up a Tool in the Console - think of it like a registered webhook with an input schema. During generation you can either have the model 'call' that tool (function) via the function-calling API, or post-validate the JSON and forward it server-side. We'll demo both.
[02:53] [03:00] Demo begins: Priya: I'm going to send a sample prompt: 'Extract order from input stream and return validated JSON conforming to schema order_v1' - hitting Redwood's JSON mode.
[03:12] [03:15] Priya (typing): "Input: Customer placed order - 2x SKU-123, 1x SKU-456, address 123 Elm St, Springfield. Return order_v1"
[03:24] System (auto): Response started streaming...
[03:30] Priya: You can see the live tokens in the Console. The model returns a JSON blob. With validation enabled, Redwood checks fields and types as they stream and flags any mismatch.
[03:43] Transcript (model output, imperfect): {
  "order_id": "ord_9a2f",
  "items": [{"sku": "SKU-123", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "SKU-456", "qty": 1}],
  "total_amount": 149.97,
  "shipping_address": {"street": "123 Elm St", "city": "Springfield", "country": "US"}
}
[04:05] Marco: That passes validation, so the function-calling hook triggers and we POST this payload to the registered webhook. You can configure retries, dead-letter queueing, and transform steps in the Console.
[04:20] Daniel: If validation fails, can we get detailed error output to retry or to surface to the user?
[04:27] Priya: Yes - Redwood returns a validation object with path, expected type, and actual value. We also log the raw tokens if you need to debug tokenization issues like KV cache misses or truncated sequences.
[04:42] Sofia: You said 'repair mode' earlier - how deterministic is that?
[04:46] Priya: Repair mode will try minimal edits to coerce types, e.g., parse numeric strings to numbers, fill missing optional fields with defaults. It's heuristic, so for strict compliance we recommend strict reject and surface the error to an orchestrator that can call the model again with a corrected prompt.
[05:05] [05:10] Daniel: What about rate limiting and backpressure? If we have bursts of orders, how do you preserve latency SLOs?
[05:16] Marco: Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching and intelligent routing. For latency-critical endpoints you can pin models to low-latency variants and configure Dedicated pools with guaranteed throughput. For hosted, we have burst limits and graceful degradation policies - e.g., fallback to a smaller model variant or enqueue with best-effort batching depending on policy.
[05:38] Alex: For your 200ms median SLO, we'd recommend a Dedicated instance with 1-2 pinned GPUs for the POC and a tuned quantization/profile for short context lengths. We'll share suggested config.
[05:51] Liam: Cost-wise how does that compare to running on our own GKE?
[05:55] Alex: We'll include a cost comparison in the pricing sheet - generally Redwood abstracts the infra and you pay usage plus any Dedicated reservation. For heavy steady-state throughput Dedicated often becomes more predictable and cheaper per unit.
[06:12] [06:20] Demo continues: Priya: Now switching to tool/function calling. I'm going to demonstrate the model emitting a call to a tool named 'create_order_webhook' with structured args rather than raw text. This is useful when you want the model to produce a payload plus an explicit intent to call the integration.
[06:39] Priya (live): Model returned: call create_order_webhook(args={"order_id":"ord_9a2f", "items":[...], "priority": "standard"})
[06:52] Marco: You can enforce schema on the args too. The Console shows the call and provides a sandbox to test webhooks.
[07:00] Daniel: Can we have secrets injected server-side so the model can't leak API keys in outputs?
[07:07] Priya: Yes - secrets are stored in the VPC/Private control plane or via KMS. The runtime never includes secret values in model-visible context unless explicitly configured.
[07:20] Sofia: We need end-to-end encryption and attestable key management for compliance.
[07:25] Priya: For Private/Dedicated deployments you can bring-your-own-key (BYOK) and HSM-backed KMS. We'll include the HSM integration notes in the security pack.
[07:42] [08:00] Daniel: Walk us through example failure modes. If the model streams partial JSON and the webhook receives it mid-stream, do you buffer?
[08:10] Marco: We buffer until validation completes. If streaming and you choose to forward mid-stream for ultra-low latency, we recommend a transform layer that can handle partials. Most customers use validated-forward so the payload is complete and conforms before delivery.
[08:30] Alex: Also note we surface token-level latency and cost in the Console so you can identify expensive prompts and optimize with Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, shorter context windows, or quantization.
[08:48] [09:00] Daniel: Tell me more about guardrails - can we block outputs that contain PII or PHI?
[09:07] Priya: Yes - you can add redactors and content filters in the pipeline. For PII we have pattern detectors and configurable redaction rules. For PHI you can integrate custom regex-based detectors or use our evals to monitor for regressions.
[09:26] Liam: Do you keep raw transcripts or user data in the hosted product? We need retention controls.
[09:33] Marco: In hosted by default we retain logs for X days per policy but you can configure retention or disable retention for sensitive streams. In Private deployment logs are under your control. We'll provide the retention matrix in the security pack.
[09:48] [10:00] Priya: Now a deeper look at the API request for JSON mode. Example curl: 
POST /v1/responses 
{
  "input": "Extract order...",
  "mode": "json",
  "schema": { ... },
  "validation": "strict",
  "function_calling": {"tool": "create_order_webhook"}
}
[10:25] Daniel: Do you version schemas? We have many downstream consumers.
[10:29] Priya: Yes - schema versioning is first-class. You can pin model-to-schema mappings and rollback across rollouts. The Console tracks schema diffs so you can see what's changed between v1 and v2.
[10:43] [11:00] Sofia: For the POC we'll probably want canary traffic and A/B compare outputs. Can Redwood do that?
[11:08] Marco: Absolutely - per-route rollouts with traffic splits, canary windows, and automatic rollback based on errors or quality regression alerts from Redwood Optimize.
[11:20] Alex: We'll set up an A/B where 10% of orders go to Redwood validated flow and 90% to your existing parser, compare success rates and latency.
[11:30] Daniel: What observability do we get for misparsed orders?
[11:34] Priya: We provide per-request traces, token-level cost, validation errors, and a sample store for flagged outputs. You can hook these into your Sentry/Datadog as well.
[11:50] [12:00] Daniel: Anything about debugging model behavior - e.g., model prefers SKU-123 = 1 even when prompt says 2?
[12:06] Marco: Evals and prompt tests are supported. Redwood Optimize can run automated test suites against prompts and detect regressions after model or quantization changes. It also surfaces prompt fingerprints that cause hallucinations.
[12:24] [12:30] Demo - advanced: Priya shows guardrail config UI where you can set validator policies (reject, repair, sanitize) and transform rules (drop fields, map keys). Then she runs a test set of messy inputs.
[13:00] Model sample output (failed case): {
  "order_id": 98231,    // numeric where string expected
  "items": "SKU-123 x2; SKU-456 x1" // unstructured string
}
[13:20] Priya: Validator flagged order_id type mismatch and items schema mismatch. Repair mode converted order_id to string and attempted to parse items into array - it succeeded for this simple case but we'd recommend manual review for ambiguous parses.
[13:36] Daniel: Good to know. For the POC we'll default to strict rejects for the first two weeks.
[13:44] [14:00] Liam: About integrations - we want the webhook to trigger internal microservices without exposing public endpoints. Can Redwood route through private peering?
[14:10] Marco: Yes - Dedicated + VPC peering or Private control plane supports private connectivity. For on-prem we can run the inference runtime in your VPC or on-prem cluster and keep control plane in a secure channel.
[14:30] Sofia: Any SDKs for Java/Kotlin? Our stack is mostly JVM.
[14:35] Priya: We have SDKs for Python, Node, and a simple HTTP contract you can call from any client. We'll share community SDKs for JVM and a sample snippet.
[14:48] [15:00] Migration question: How do you handle schema evolution without downtime?
[15:06] Marco: Use versioned schemas and per-route model + schema mapping. You can roll new schema to a subset of traffic and use the Console to compare. If the new schema fails, automatic rollback can be configured.
[15:22] Alex: Quick note on costs: repair mode does extra tokens for retrying or reparsing, so it can increase cost. Strict reject cost is just the validation pass. We'll itemize that in pricing.
[15:36] [16:00] Daniel: OK show us the API logs and demo a failed validation alert.
[16:08] Priya: Switching to logs. (screen) Here's a request that failed validation - details show the failing path, the raw tokens and the suggested repair. You can configure alerts to create a ticket in Jira automatically.
[16:30] Daniel: Nice. For POC we'll want automatic tickets for rejects.
[16:36] Priya: We can configure that.
[16:40] [17:00] Security deep dive: Liam: For auditability we need immutable logs with time-stamped events.
[17:07] Marco: Redwood provides append-only audit logs and tamper-evidence features in Private control plane. For Hosted we can provide signed logs on request. We'll include options in the security docs.
[17:25] [18:00] Daniel: Latency: if we have a cold KV cache, will token generation spike?
[18:10] Marco: Cold KV misses can add overhead for long-context models. For short order payloads KV cache isn't a major factor; it's more relevant to long chat contexts. We'll tune the model and kernel selection for your workload.
[18:30] [19:00] Wrap-up demo: Priya runs final end-to-end where model validates, calls the create_order_webhook tool, and the Console shows the successful delivery with HTTP 200.
[19:22] Daniel: That looked solid. Couple of questions: can we run synthetic load to simulate peak concurrency?
[19:30] Alex: Yes, Redwood has a load test harness we can run during the POC to replicate your qps and payload distribution. We'll include that in the POC plan.
[19:45] Sofia: Any gotchas for multi-tenant merchants? We have multiple brands under one account.
[19:51] Marco: You can use route-level configs and per-tenant API keys, RBAC, and schema scoping. The Console supports per-route dashboards to isolate metrics.
[20:06] [20:30] Next steps and recap: Alex: To recap - we'll send pricing and Dedicated recommendations, Priya will send the security pack, and we'll set up a POC window for the week of 2027-03-29. Customer to provide sample prompt set and SLOs.
[20:50] Daniel: Sounds good. One last ask - can you include a short runbook for handling validation rejects?
[20:56] Priya: Yes we'll include a runbook and sample retry logic.
[21:05] Liam: Thanks everyone.
[21:10] Alex: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with the docs and scheduling links.
[21:16] (call ends)

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings and tokenization artifacts. Refer to raw Console logs for exact tokens.
